newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees rebels taking Kinshasa in a day or two.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees rebels taking Kinshasa in a day or two.

text.p: U.S. officials said on Monday that it may only be one or two days before rebels led by Laurent Kabila take over the Zairean capital, Kinshasa.

Rebel forces were reported to be 38-62 miles (60-100 km) from Kinshasa -- only "a day or two" if Kabila decided to invade the city, one official told Reuters, adding: "He'll be coming. There's no doubt about it."
Kabila met ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko on a South African navy ship on Sunday. They disagreed on arrangements for Mobutu to step down but agreed to meet again within 10 days.
Mobutu wants to hand over power to some transitional body while Kabila wants to take over full control immediately.

U.S. officials told Reuters that as one condition for his departure, Mobutu said in a letter to President Bill Clinton, that if he left power he wanted assurances "some of his financial resources would remain intact."
"We can't deliver that for him," one official said.
He said this and other demands made by Mobutu may "become moot ... (because) Kabila is going to be marching into Kinshasa in a few days."
For that same reason, talk of another Kabila-Mobutu meeting in eight to 10 days may also be moot.

Kabila told his own news conference earlier: "If Mobutu hands over power before we enter Kinshasa, I will guarantee his safety and that of his biological family. But if he does not, we will have to chase him away in humiliation."
That is why U.S. envoy Bill Richardson was in Lumubashi, Zaire, on Monday pushing for a "soft landing" without bloodshed when the rebels enter Kinshasa, U.S. officials said.
John Dinger, a State Department spokesman, said Richardson's schedule was flexible and open-ended.

With events in Central Africa "moving very quickly," Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, aimed to reinforce South Africa's peace initiative on Zaire in any way South African President Nelson Mandela wanted, Dinger said.
Richardson met Rwandan military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame on Monday before seeing Kabila and would next see Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni who is visiting Botswana.

Rwanda and Uganda are key backers of the Tutsi-dominated rebels led by Kabila. U.S. officials said Richardson would urge them to convince Kabila on the need for "an inclusive transitional government leading to elections."

The United States is not insisting that Mobutu or his allies must be part of that arrangement but is suggesting that other elements of Zaire's political opposition, not just Kabila's forces, could be involved, U.S. officials said.
Dinger refused to say if the United States, which during the Cold War was a strong ally of Mobutu, planned a reconstruction package to help rebuild Zaire.

But another official told Reuters planning is not yet at that stage. "Before we consider a package of assistance there has to be a new democratically elected government in Zaire ... We're a long way off from that," he said.

In addition to civil war, Mobutu is battling cancer. One U.S. official described him as looking "pretty frail" and said Mobutu has been "unable to stand without help (and so) has been mostly in bed. He's been receiving visitors in bed." He could not predict how long Mobutu might have to live.

Troops from the United States, Belgium, France and Britain are waiting in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate Western nationals from the teeming capital of 5 million people in the event of trouble.

The United States ordered the departure over the weekend of non-essential personnel. As a result, nine personnel departed Kinshasa and travelled by ferry to Brazzaville, Congo, leaving 39 official Americans in the capital.

Kabila's rebels, seven months into a military offensive from the east, control three quarters of the country. The Zairean Army has put up minimal resistance and Mobutu's foreign friends have largely abandoned him.
